plain: An air tank that holds the air used by the service brakes.
The pressure at which the air governor stops the compressor from adding more air.
Antilock braking system, which helps keep the wheels from locking up in hard braking.
Gross vehicle weight rating, the most weight a vehicle is built to carry, set by the maker.
Watched by a person who is on the vehicle awake, or close by with a clear view.
A part that keeps the brakes adjusted on its own as the linings wear.
When a trailer comes loose from the vehicle towing it.
A large container, such as a cargo tank, that holds hazmat without smaller inner packages.
A permit that lets you practice driving a commercial vehicle on public roads with a CDL holder beside you.
Reflective tape or reflectors that help other drivers see a trailer at night.
The hardware that joins a truck and a trailer, such as a fifth wheel or pintle hook.
A period when you lose the right to drive a commercial vehicle.
A brake system that can stop the vehicle if the service brakes fail.
Information that tells responders the hazards of a material and what to do in a spill, fire or leak.
An added permission on a CDL that lets you drive a certain kind of vehicle or load.
Being so tired that your alertness and reaction time are lower.
The coupling plate on a tractor that holds the trailer's kingpin.
A code, such as 10 B:C, that shows how much fire an extinguisher can fight.
A phone you hold in your hand to talk. Federal rules ban using one while driving a CMV.
The four-way flashing lights that warn other drivers your vehicle is stopped.
Materials that can hurt people or property if they are not handled safely, such as fuel, gases and chemicals.
Federal limits on how long a driver may drive and work.
A serious violation, such as leaving the scene of an accident, that brings a long disqualification.
A company that moves goods or people by commercial vehicle.
Smaller packages such as boxes, drums and cylinders.
All the time you are working or ready to work for a carrier, not just time spent driving.
An order that stops you from driving until a problem is fixed or a set time has passed.
A Roman numeral (I, II or III) that shows how dangerous a hazardous material is.
The brake that holds the vehicle still when parked.
A full inspection of a commercial vehicle that must be done at least once every 12 months.
A hook coupling used to pull a full trailer or dolly.
A diamond-shaped sign on a vehicle that shows the hazard class of the load.
A layer of cord fabric inside a tire.
The official name of a hazardous material, shown on the shipping paper.
The rod that moves out of the brake chamber to apply the brake.
A bar across the rear of a trailer that helps stop a car from sliding underneath.
An air tank that stores air for the brakes.
The straps, chains and other gear that hold cargo in place.
Keeping hazardous materials apart so they cannot react with each other.
A violation such as speeding 15 mph or more over the limit that brings a disqualification if it happens more than once in 3 years.
The brakes you use to slow and stop the vehicle while driving.
The front axle that turns the vehicle.
The air tank that feeds air to the brakes on a trailer.
Trailer brakes that apply on their own when the towing vehicle slows.
Typing or reading text on a phone or other device.
A valve that closes to keep the truck's air if the trailer's air line breaks or leaks.
A written report of defects the driver found or was told about on a vehicle.
Reflective triangles or flares you place on the road to warn traffic about a stopped vehicle.
